name: Sarecycline (Seysara)

lead: Sarecycline (Seysara) is an oral tetracycline antibiotic approved by the FDA in October 2018 for inflammatory lesions of non-nodular moderate to severe acne in people aged 9 and older. People take it to clear red, inflamed breakouts on the face and, often, the body.

It blocks bacterial protein synthesis and was designed as a narrow-spectrum drug aimed mainly at the skin bacterium Cutibacterium acnes, with little activity against common gut bacteria, which differs from older tetracyclines like doxycycline and minocycline. Safety and efficacy data from the pivotal trials are summarised in published reviews.

paras: It is a once-daily tablet taken under a prescriber's supervision. Guidelines for oral acne antibiotics generally advise keeping courses to about three months because of resistance concerns.

As a tetracycline-class antibiotic it is prescription-only and used under medical supervision. Antibiotic resistance is a recognised concern with any oral acne antibiotic, which is why courses are time-limited.

angle.text: Sarecycline is a once-daily prescription tetracycline that targets acne bacteria and inflammation, so fewer inflamed lesions appear on the face and body. It was approved for moderate to severe inflammatory acne in 2018 and has been studied in acne trials.

lead: Sarecycline, sold in the United States under the brand name Seysara, is an oral tetracycline-class antibiotic approved for acne vulgaris. The FDA approved the tablet formulation in early October 2018 for the treatment of inflammatory lesions of non-nodular moderate to severe acne in patients aged 9 years and older [1][2].

It was developed by Paratek and Allergan and later acquired by the dermatology-focused company Almirall [1]. It is described as a narrow-spectrum tetracycline, meaning that it is aimed mainly at Cutibacterium acnes and has little activity against the Gram-negative bacteria typical of the human gut [2].

Sarecycline is a conventional prescription acne medicine rather than a product that originated in looksmaxxing culture. The sources reviewed for this article contain no substantial forum discussion of it. Its inclusion in the wiki reflects its place among oral options for acne, a common concern in skin-focused appearance discussions.

paras: The approved indication is the inflammatory lesions of non-nodular moderate to severe acne vulgaris in patients aged 9 and older [1][2]. Its label does not cover non-inflammatory lesions (comedones) as a treatment target.
Small investigator-run studies have registered the drug for other skin conditions, including rosacea and perioral (periorificial) dermatitis, and for truncal acne [3][4][5]. These are off-label uses.

Wikipedia reports that two randomized, well-controlled phase 3 trials evaluated sarecycline on facial and truncal acne in a combined group of about 2,000 participants, using a once-daily weight-based dose [2]. A systematic review of the published clinical trials examined the efficacy and safety data from these studies [6], and a physician-oriented review describes its place alongside other oral tetracyclines [7].

A 2021 registered study, the Patient-reported Outcomes for Sarecycline Effectiveness and Safety (PROSES) trial, enrolled 300 participants with acne and has been completed [8]. Published numerical results are not summarised here.

Safety and tolerability data from the pivotal trials are summarised in published reviews and in a family-physician guide to the drug [6][7]. Specific adverse-event rates are not reproduced here; prescribers consult the product label.

Sarecycline inhibits bacterial protein synthesis. Unlike earlier tetracyclines, its long C7 side chain reaches toward the bacterial messenger RNA and forms hydrogen bonds with nucleotides [2]. It targets clinically relevant Gram-positive organisms, chiefly C. acnes, with little or no activity against typical Gram-negative gut bacteria [2].

Sarecycline has the molecular formula C24H29N3O8 and a molar mass of about 487.5 g/mol. One reported synthesis starts from sancycline and proceeds through palladium-catalysed carbonylation and reductive amination, with an overall yield of about 23% [2].
Sarecycline is prescription-only in the United States [2].
Seysara is the brand name. The compound was previously known by the code P-005672 [2].

Human trials exist. Two phase 3 randomized trials supported the 2018 US approval [1][2], and a systematic review has summarised the published trial literature [6]. Later registered studies include PROSES in 300 acne patients, a 10-person truncal acne study, a 100-participant pilot study in rosacea and a 9-participant study in perioral dermatitis [3][4][5][8].

timeline.event: The FDA approves sarecycline tablets (Seysara) for inflammatory lesions of moderate to severe acne in patients aged 9 and older [1][2].
A first global approval review and a Medical Letter commentary describe the drug [1][7].
The PROSES patient-reported outcomes study begins [8].
